translation: Perhaps because Miho and Satsuki spend so much time together locally, they share similar expressions and speaking styles.
They especially have similar ways of eating sweets, each breaking off small pieces of cookies with their manicured hands to put to their mouths.
I try to remember if it was always like this, but my memories are hazy.
I think the little habits and gestures they had when we last met might have drifted away somewhere by now.
Miho is now married, owns a used single-family house in her hometown, and often hosts her friends there.

Sometimes she feels reluctant about going to her part-time job the next day, but it's her only connection to a world beyond the convenience store and a valuable opportunity to interact with other "normal thirty-somethings".
So she tries to accept Miho's invitations as much as possible.
Today as well, Miho, Yukari who brought her little child along, Satsuki who is married but doesn't have children yet and me have gathered at Miho's place with cakes for tea time.
That was when I became a part of the world for the first time.
At that moment, I felt as though I had truly been born.
On this day, as a functioning part of the world, I was undeniably born.
For two weeks before the grand opening, we found ourselves in pairs, undergoing constant practice with unnamed prospective customers.
We learned to look the "customer" in the eye and give a courtesy smile, put sanitary products in a paper bag separately, place hot items apart from cold ones.
We were also taught to sanitize our hands upon receiving an order for fast food.
To familiarize us with handling money, actual currency was kept inside the register; however, each receipt bore a large "training" imprint.
The experience somewhat resembled playing pretend-store since the individuals on either side of transactions were fellow part-time workers wearing matching uniforms.
My younger sister, two years my junior, was a "normal" child unlike me.
That is not to say she kept her distance from me, quite the opposite; she looked up to me.
Whenever my sister got scolded by our mother over mundane things that differed from my behavior, I would approach our mother and ask "Why are you angry?"
Once the lecture was done because of my question, and possibly feeling that I had defended her, my sister would always thank me by saying "Thank you".
Having not much interest in sweets or toys myself, I often gave them to her instead.
For this reason she was always following after me.
"Dad likes yakitori, so let's grill this and eat it today.
Not hearing a response, I repeated my statement clearly.
My mother was taken aback, as was the other child's mother next to her; her eyes, nostrils, and mouth all opened wide in surprise.
Her strange expression almost made me laugh but then I noticed her focus on what was in my hand and realized one bird wouldn't be enough.
"Should I get more?"
As I glanced at two or three sparrows walking nearby, my mother came back to her senses and cried out desperately at me: "Keiko!"
"We should bury the little birdy instead see everyone is crying because they lost their friend.
It must be really sad.
"Why? It's already dead anyway.
My question rendered my mother speechless.
He quickly put a can of coffee, some cigarettes, and an American hot dog into a small-size bag.
Meanwhile, the man who had been jingling coins in his pocket suddenly reaches into his breast pocket as if he just remembered something.
From this gesture, I immediately inferred that he was going to pay with electronic money.
"Welcome, good morning!"
I take the can of coffee that the male customer offers with a light bow.
"Ah, and one pack of no. 5 cigarettes.
"Certainly.
I quickly pull out a pack of Marlboro Light Menthol and scan it at the register.
"May I please have you confirm your age on screen?"
As he is touching the screen, I notice his gaze swiftly move to the showcase filled with fast food and stop my hand motion.
Though I could offer assistance asking, "Would you like anything else?" when customers seem to be contemplating whether or not to make an additional purchase, my policy is step back and wait.
At the faint jingle of loose change, I turn around, eyes directed at the cash register.
People who juggle coins in their palm or pocket often are simply here to buy cigarettes or newspapers and leave promptly, so I am attuned to the sound of money.
Sure enough, there is a man approaching the register with a can of coffee in one hand while his other hand rummages through his pocket.
Swiftly moving within the store, I slide behind the counter to ensure I'm ready and don't keep our customers waiting.
A convenience store is filled with sounds.
The chime when a customer enters, the voice of an idol advertising new products over the store's PA system.
Shouts from the staff, the beep of the barcode scanner.
The sound of items being put into a basket, crinkling of bread bags and clicking heels pacing within the store.
All these blend together to create "the sound of a convenience store" that constantly resonates in my ears.
